summary: Describes several problems found with the SIP non-INVITE transaction. It is an informational background document that sets out the issues which other work then addresses.

plainLanguage.summary: A SIP transaction that is not an INVITE has a fixed lifetime, so the server must answer quickly or the client gives up first. RFC 4321 lists six ways this goes wrong, from the client and server disagreeing about the outcome to a server sending a rejection that reaches the caller long after it stopped listening.

what are sip non-invite transaction problems
how does provisional response affect recovery
what is the non-invite race condition
subtitle: Six edge cases in which a SIP request that is not an INVITE can time out, be ignored, or be answered too late to be useful.

tldr.problem: A SIP non-INVITE transaction has a fixed, finite duration, so anything that answers slowly or not at all leaves the two ends disagreeing about what happened.
tldr.mechanism: The document works through the resulting problems: the race between a final response and the client timeout, the way a provisional response delays recovery, the need to blacklist a server that answers too slowly, the useless 408 response, the effect on forking proxies, and the damage done by mismatched timer settings.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational document that states the problems rather than fixing them. The solutions are in the companion document RFC 4320.

today: RFC 4321 is an Informational document from January 2006 and has not been obsoleted or updated. It states the problems with the SIP non-INVITE transaction rather than fixing them; the corresponding actions are in RFC 4320.

sections.title: Six Problems With the Non-INVITE Transaction
sections.content:
The SIP non-INVITE transaction is the transaction model used for SIP requests other than INVITE, such as the requests that begin transactions. A number of unpleasant edge conditions are created by its fixed duration, and the negative aspects of some of them are made worse by the effect that provisional responses have on the non-INVITE transaction state machines as currently defined.

The document lists six problems. A non-INVITE transaction must complete immediately or it risks losing a race against the client's timeout. Provisional responses can delay recovery from a lost final response. Delayed responses will temporarily blacklist an element. The 408 response is not useful for a non-INVITE. Non-INVITE timeouts doom forking proxies. And mismatched timer values make winning the race harder.

The document states the problems only. The solutions are defined in the companion document, RFC 4320.
sections.plainLanguage: A SIP transaction that is not an INVITE has to finish quickly, because it is given only a fixed amount of time. The document lists the six ways that fixed limit causes trouble.

sections.title: The Race Every Non-INVITE Can Lose
sections.content:
The non-INVITE transaction defined in RFC 3261 is designed to have a fixed and finite duration, dependent on the timer T1. A consequence of this design is that participants must strive to complete the transaction as quickly as possible.

Consider the race condition in Figure 1. The User Agent Server believes it has responded to the request in time, and that the request succeeded. The User Agent Client, on the other hand, believes the request has timed out and therefore failed. No longer having a matching client transaction, the client core ignores what it believes to be a spurious response. As far as the client is concerned, it received no response at all. The result is that the two ends have conflicting views of the outcome.

A UAS therefore cannot wait until the last possible moment to send a final response. It must send its response so that it arrives at the client before that client times out. Unfortunately the UAS has no way to measure the propagation time of the request accurately, or predict the propagation time of the response, and the uncertainty is compounded by each proxy that takes part in the transaction. Its only choice is to send the final response as soon as it can and hope for the best.

This constrains the set of problems a single non-INVITE can solve. Any delay introduced while processing the request increases the probability of losing the race. If the timing of that processing is not predictable and controllable, a single transaction is an inappropriate model for handling the request. One viable alternative is to accept the request with a 202 and send the ultimate results in a new request in the reciprocal direction. In specialised networks, a UAS might have reliable knowledge of inter-hop latency and use it to decide whether it has time to delay its final response for a database lookup, but establishing that knowledge across arbitrary networks, perhaps using resource reservation techniques and deterministic transports, is not currently feasible.
sections.plainLanguage: The server and the client each have a timer running. If the server's reply crosses the line just after the client has given up, the server thinks it succeeded and the client thinks it failed, and the client discards the reply as a stray message.

sections.title: Provisional Responses Delay Recovery
sections.content:
The non-INVITE client transaction state machine provides reliability for these transactions over unreliable transports such as UDP through retransmission of the request message. Timer E is set to T1 when a request is initially transmitted. As long as the machine remains in the Trying state, each time Timer E fires it is reset to twice its previous value, capped at T2, and the request is retransmitted.

If the state machine sees a provisional response it transitions to the Proceeding state, where retransmission continues but the algorithm for resetting Timer E is simply to use T2 instead of doubling at each firing. Timer E is not altered during the transition to Proceeding.

Making that transition before Timer E has been reset to T2 can make recovery from a lost final response take extra time. Recovery occurs within 2*T1 in the case without a provisional message. With a provisional response, recovery is delayed until T2, which by default is 8*T1. No additional delay is introduced if the first provisional response is received after Timer E has already reached its maximum reset interval of T2.

In practical terms, a provisional response to a non-INVITE in currently deployed networks can delay transaction completion by up to 3.5 seconds.
sections.plainLanguage: When the client is still resending the request, it backs off faster each time. But if the server sends an interim reply, the client stops backing off and settles on the long interval, so a lost final reply is not noticed for much longer.

sections.title: A Slow Server Gets Blacklisted
sections.content:
RFC 3263 specifies how a SIP element uses DNS Service Record resource records, and it discusses how SIP ensures high availability by having upstream elements detect the failure of downstream elements. Two behaviours matter here. Within a transaction, transport failure is detected either through an explicit report from the transport layer or through timeout, and timeout indicates transport failure regardless of the transport in use. When transport failure is detected, the request is retried at the next element from the sorted results of the SRV query. Between transactions, locations reporting temporary failure, for example through a 503 with Retry-After, are not used until their requested black-out period expires.

The specification notes the benefit of caching locations that are successfully contacted, but does not discuss how such a cache is maintained. It is unclear whether an element should stop using, that is temporarily blacklist, a location returned in the SRV query that results in a transport error, and if so, when the location should be removed from the blacklist.

Without such a blacklist the intended availability mechanism fails miserably. Consider traffic between two domains. A proxy in domain A has to forward a sequence of non-INVITE requests to domain B. Through DNS SRV it discovers pB1 and pB2, and the ordering rules indicate it should use pB1 first. The first request to pB1 times out. Since a non-INVITE transaction has a fixed duration, the proxy has no opportunity to retry the request at pB2 within that transaction. If the proxy does not remember pB1's failure, the second request, and all subsequent non-INVITE requests until pB1 recovers, are doomed to the same failure. Caching would allow the subsequent requests to be tried at pB2.

Since such failure is not acceptable in deployed networks, elements are expected to cache timeout failures between transactions. Then the race described earlier becomes important: an element that fails to respond soon enough has effectively not responded at all, and will be blacklisted at its peer for some period. Even with caching, the first request timeout still results in a timeout failure all the way back to the original submitter, because the failover mechanisms of RFC 3263 increase the resiliency of an INVITE transaction but do nothing for a given non-INVITE transaction.
sections.plainLanguage: Servers are found through a DNS lookup that returns a ranked list. If the first one on the list does not answer, the proxy should remember that and try the next one for later requests, because a non-INVITE cannot be retried inside the same transaction.

sections.title: Late Responses, Forking Proxies and Mismatched Timers
sections.content:
408 for a non-INVITE is not useful. Most existing endpoints emit a 408 for a non-INVITE request 64*T1 after receiving the request if they have not emitted an earlier final response, and such a 408 is guaranteed to arrive at the next upstream element too late to be useful. In the presence of proxies the messages are even harmful: by the time the 408 arrives, each proxy has already terminated its client transaction due to timeout, so each proxy must forward the 408 upstream statelessly, and that too arrives too late. The result can be the original requester being bombarded with spurious 408s. The proxy's client transaction state machine never enters the Completed state, so Timer K does not come into play. This response bombardment is not limited to the 408, though it only exists when participating client transaction state machines are timing out, and it can even affect a successful response: even though the server responds in time to the last proxy, the response is too late for the proxies in between and for the client.

Non-INVITE timeouts doom forking proxies. A single branch with a delayed or missing final response dominates the processing at a proxy that receives no 2xx responses to a forked non-INVITE request. This proxy is required to allow all of its client transactions to terminate before choosing a best response, which forces the proxy's server transaction to lose the race described earlier. Any response it ultimately forwards, a 401 for example, arrives at the upstream elements too late to be used. So if no element among the branches would return a 2xx response, the failure of a single element or its transport dooms the proxy to failure.

Mismatched timer values make winning the race harder. There are many failure scenarios due to misconfiguration or misbehaviour that the SIP specification does not discuss. One is placing two elements with different configured values for T1 and T2 on the same network. The race failure only becomes more likely in that state, and it may appear that shortening T1 at the element behaving as the server improves the situation, but these elements may trade roles on the next request. Since the protocol provides no mechanism for discovering or negotiating a peer's timer values, exceptional care must be taken when deploying systems with non-default values, to ensure they never communicate directly with elements using default values.
sections.plainLanguage: Three further problems follow. The rejection a server sends after its own timeout arrives long after the caller stopped waiting, so it is wasted work and can be used to flood a caller. A proxy that sent the same request to several servers has to wait for all of them, so one slow server dooms it. And two machines with different timeout settings lose the race more often than two that agree.

sections.title: Why These Problems Matter for Security
sections.content:
The problems described are in the core SIP specification and concern the SIP requests other than INVITE that begin transactions. A few of them lead to flooding or forgery risk, and could possibly be exploited by an adversary in a denial of service attack. Solutions are defined in the companion document, RFC 4320.

One solution there prohibits proxies and user agents from sending 408 responses to non-INVITE transactions. Without this change, proxies automatically generate a storm of useless responses. An attacker could capitalise on this by enticing user agents to send non-INVITE requests to a black hole, through social engineering or DNS poisoning, or by selectively dropping responses.

Another solution prohibits proxies from forwarding late responses. Without this change, an attacker could easily forge messages which appear to be late responses. All proxies compliant with RFC 3261 are required to forward these responses, wasting bandwidth and processor time and potentially overwhelming target user agents, especially those with low speed connections.
sections.plainLanguage: Two of these problems can be turned into an attack. A flood of late rejections wastes the caller's resources, and a forged late response can make every proxy in the path work hard for nothing. The companion document stops both.

viz.caption: THE TIMERS THAT GOVERN A NON-INVITE TRANSACTION

items.label: Initial retransmission interval
items.desc: Timer E is set to T1 when the request is first transmitted, and is doubled on each firing while in the Trying state.

items.label: Maximum retransmission interval
items.desc: Timer E is capped at T2, and by default T2 is 8*T1.

items.label: Transaction duration
items.desc: The fixed, finite duration of a non-INVITE transaction, and the delay before an endpoint emits a 408.

items.label: Recovery without a provisional
items.desc: Recovery from a lost final response occurs within this time when no provisional response has been received.

items.label: Worst-case delay
items.desc: How much a provisional response can delay completion of a non-INVITE in currently deployed networks.

items.title: The 408 arrives too late
items.text: A 408 emitted 64*T1 after the request reaches the next element after its own transaction has already timed out, so it must be forwarded statelessly and arrives after the requester stopped waiting.

items.title: Forking proxies wait for the slowest branch
items.text: A proxy that sent the request to several servers must let all of its client transactions terminate before choosing a best response, so one failed branch dooms the whole proxy.

items.title: Mismatched timers make the race worse
items.text: Two elements with different T1 and T2 values on the same network lose the race more often, and SIP has no way to discover or negotiate a peer's timer values.
